title: As the US pulls its forces out of Iraq, what happens to Iran-backed armed groups?
gist: As the US completes its withdrawal from Iraq 23 years after the invasion, the most powerful Iran-aligned armed groups — Kataeb Hezbollah, Harakat al-Nujaba and Kataeb Sayyid al-Shuhada — reject PM Ali al-Zaidi's new 30 June 2027 disarmament deadline. Experts doubt the state can rein them in, warn forced disarmament risks clashes or civil war, and say any integration would take years and need Iran's assent.

insights.claim: Iraqi PM Ali al-Zaidi framed October 1 as a day the country would be free of any foreign military presence, but Turkey still maintains forces in Iraq, though it has pledged to hand over its Bashiqa-Zilkan base.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Official 'full sovereignty' claims overstate reality; Turkish presence remains a residual friction point.
insights.locator: His statement is not quite accurate

insights.claim: The end of the US presence was originally tied to disarming extra-government armed groups, but the disarmament deadline was pushed to 30 June 2027 while the troop exit went ahead on 30 September.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Decoupling troop exit from disarmament removes US leverage — mid-2027 becomes the next flashpoint.
insights.locator: The end of the US presence

insights.claim: Kataeb Hezbollah, Harakat al-Nujaba and Kataeb Sayyid al-Shuhada — the most powerful armed groups — have said they will not disarm or come under state control.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Core Iran-aligned militias remain armed, sustaining risk of attacks on US and Israeli assets from Iraq.
insights.locator: But the most powerful of these groups

insights.claim: CNAS's Hamzeh Hadad distinguishes groups whose leaders see a political future, which may realistically disarm and integrate, from those whose raison d'etre is fighting for Iran's regional vision, which the state will struggle to address.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Expect partial, uneven disarmament — the Iran-aligned hard core is the residual risk.
insights.quote: For the other armed groups, they have a different raison d’être, which is fighting for Iran’s political vision throughout the region.

insights.claim: Although formally part of the state-sanctioned Popular Mobilisation Forces, the most powerful groups are effectively independent, mostly loyal to Iran, and deeply embedded in Iraq's political establishment, military and organised crime.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Militia entrenchment in politics and economy limits reform and keeps governance/corruption risk high in Iraq.
insights.locator: But the most powerful armed groups are older

insights.claim: Several groups united as the Islamic Resistance in Iraq to target Israeli and US assets over the war in Gaza, and supporters celebrated the US withdrawal as won through 'the blood of the martyrs'.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Militias claim victory, which may embolden further action against US/Israeli interests.
insights.locator: In recent years, a number of them

themes.theme: Civil-war and economic risk from disarmament

insights.claim: Activist Hisham al-Mozani warns that forcing disarmament could bring army-militia clashes and even a return to civil war, damaging Iraq's economy and security.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: A forced disarmament push is a tail risk for Iraqi stability and oil production.
insights.quote: For the army and security forces, maybe they will have clashes with the militias and that's a very, very dangerous thing - it will affect the economy, affect security in all of Iraq

insights.claim: Al-Mozani estimates disarming and integrating the militias would take around five years even if it began, because some date back to the 1980 Iran-Iraq war and sit in parties, parliament and ministries — and Iran would ultimately have to approve.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: The June 2027 deadline is likely unrealistic; Iranian influence over the process persists.
insights.locator: He said he believed the process

insights.claim: Former human-rights commissioner Ali al-Bayati is not optimistic the state can rein in the groups and sees every chance the US could return to Iraq in future, as it did after 2011.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: US re-engagement in Iraq remains a live scenario if security deteriorates.

insights.claim: With the Israeli-US war on Iran raging, the US is increasing pressure on Baghdad to rein in Iran-linked forces, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio warning Iraq risks 'Balkanisation' if it does not.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Rising US pressure raises odds of sanctions or coercive measures on Iraq tied to Iran links.
insights.locator: However, with the Israeli-US war on Iran

insights.claim: Ali al-Bayati argues militia power stems partly from the US failure after 2003 to build professional security and military institutions despite huge budgets, which allowed IS to seize a third of Iraq.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Weak state institutions are the root vulnerability; expect militias to fill any security vacuum.
insights.quote: they failed to form professional security and military institutions in spite of huge budgets
insights.locator: Bayati, who now lives in Switzerland
